steps.thought: I'd like something that actually stretches my tact rather than another shopping dialogue.

args.text: I'd like to practise disagreeing with a senior designer in a critique and giving difficult feedback without sounding blunt. Also, turning down after-work drinks gracefully, a bit of Irish office banter, and dealing with a pushy landlord at a flat viewing in Dublin.

topicsShown.title: Disagreeing with a senior designer
topicsShown.goal: Challenge a design choice while acknowledging its strengths and keeping the critique collaborative.
topicsShown.why: You want to disagree with a senior designer without sounding blunt.

topicsShown.title: Giving feedback that is hard to hear
topicsShown.goal: Explain a recurring problem, describe its impact fairly, and agree on a specific change.
topicsShown.why: This gives you practice being tactful without making difficult feedback too vague.

topicsShown.title: Saying no to after-work drinks
topicsShown.goal: Decline drinks warmly and firmly without giving a personal explanation or an unintended promise.
topicsShown.why: You specifically want to turn down after-work drinks while keeping things friendly.

topicsShown.title: Making sense of vague design feedback
topicsShown.goal: Turn an ambiguous critique into concrete criteria without sounding defensive.
topicsShown.why: Clarifying what someone means gives you firmer ground for responding to difficult feedback.

topicsShown.title: Agreeing what to change before launch
topicsShown.goal: Negotiate a limited revision plan that balances design concerns, time, and shared priorities.
topicsShown.why: You can turn disagreement into a practical agreement instead of leaving the critique unresolved.

topicsShown.title: Explaining why you changed your mind
topicsShown.goal: Recount a design disagreement, distinguish evidence from assumptions, and explain your revised view.
topicsShown.why: Explaining a change of mind helps you stay credible and flexible during critiques.

topicsShown.title: Viewing a flat in Dublin
topicsShown.goal: Ask probing questions about a flat and politely hold your ground when the landlord wants an immediate decision.
topicsShown.why: You asked to practise awkward rental questions and staying polite but firm under pressure.

topicsShown.title: A bit of banter in the Dublin office
topicsShown.goal: Respond to dry humour, try gentle teasing, and shift smoothly into a professional register.
topicsShown.why: You asked to explore Irish office banter, idioms, and where friendly teasing should stop.

criteria.evidence: #1 shows "C1 · Fluent", but this journey contains no placement tasks or assessed placement verdict.
#1–#6 contain topic planning, with no check tasks.
#6 ends at "Next from your plan"; no partner conversation occurs.

All six initial topics in facts.topicsShown concern workplace or social nuance, exceeding four of six. #3 includes "Disagreeing with a senior designer", "Giving feedback that is hard to hear", and "Saying no to after-work drinks".
#6 provides a next-topic preview, not a placement verdict summary.

boundaries.notes: No defined breach appears in #1–#6 or the eight proposed topics.

findings.title: Initial suggestions omit two explicitly requested situations
findings.expected: The first six topics cover Jana's requested mix of design, social and Dublin relocation situations.
findings.got: Five initial topics centre on design work. Jana must repeat her landlord and Irish banter requests through two additions.
findings.evidence: #2 requests "Irish office banter" and "a pushy landlord at a flat viewing in Dublin". Neither appears in the initial six facts.topicsShown entries. #3: "apparently my entire life happens in a design critique". #4: "I still want some Irish office banter".
findings.suggested_acceptance: Cover all five explicitly requested situations within the initial six suggestions before adding adjacent design scenarios.

findings.title: Custom additions preserve the practical nuance
findings.expected: Added topics retain the pressure, interpersonal stakes and register Jana requested.
findings.got: Both additions preserve their central intent and appear in the agreed plan.
findings.evidence: #3 requests "resisting pressure to commit on the spot"; facts.topicsShown retains "politely hold your ground when the landlord wants an immediate decision". #4 requests "teasing people without overstepping"; the resulting goal includes "try gentle teasing, and shift smoothly into a professional register". #5 agrees: "That's a pretty solid mix".
findings.suggested_acceptance: Preserve these constraints and named settings when converting free-text requests into agreed topics.

findings.title: Relevant explanations and a clear handoff
findings.expected: Jana understands the topic choices and can tell that agreeing worked.
findings.got: Topics explain their interpersonal purpose, and the home screen identifies the next agreed activity.
findings.evidence: #3 explains feedback practice as "being tactful without making difficult feedback too vague" and offers "Swap any you don't want, add your own in your words, then agree". #6 shows "Next from your plan: Disagreeing with a senior designer".
findings.suggested_acceptance: Keep concrete purpose statements and the explicit next-topic confirmation.

judge.voice:
I'd use this plan. Disagreeing without sounding blunt and declining drinks without accidentally promising next time are exactly my sort of problems. The first batch did make my life look like one endless design critique. I'd already asked for the landlord and Irish banter, so repeating both was mildly annoying. Once added, though, they kept the awkward bits I actually wanted to practise.

I trust the relevance of the finished plan. I haven't heard the partner or seen a correction, so C1 on the home screen doesn't yet convince me this can replace my tutor. There is no wait timing here to judge, either. Swapping was offered, but I didn't try it. I'd tell a colleague the topic planning looks useful; I'd want an actual Dublin conversation before recommending the teaching.
